lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: understand that polarisation of anions by cations leads to some covalency in an ionic bond, based on evidence from the Born-Haber cycle

primer.text: Perfect ionic crystals assume spherical ions and pure electrostatic attraction, but small, highly charged cations can distort a big anion's electron cloud - polarisation - and every distortion threads covalent character into the bond, moving the measured lattice energy off the theoretical value. This note defines polarising power and polarisability and explains the lattice-energy gap.

modules.title: When ionic bonds borrow covalent character
modules.opening: Theoretical lattice energies price a perfect ionic model: wholly spherical ions, purely electrostatic attraction, whole-number charges exchanged once and forever. Real anions can be squashed out of shape - polarised - when a cation drags on their electron density, and that distortion threads covalent character into the bond, splitting the measured lattice energy away from the calculated one.
keyPoints: Calculating a theoretical lattice energy assumes a perfect ionic model: wholly spherical ions with purely electrostatic attractions.
The model assumes a complete, irreversible exchange of outer-shell electrons giving whole-number ionic charges.
Measured lattice energy can differ from the theoretical value.
Polarisation of the anion introduces covalent character into the bond.
The cation attracts electrons from the anion, distorting the anion's electron density.

low.restatement: The maths of a perfect ionic crystal assumes round ions tugging only electrostatically; when a small positive ion squashes a negative ion's electron cloud, the bond quietly gains some sharing character.
low.analogy: Two billiard balls rolling together stay a pure collision; press one ball into a putty ball and the pair starts behaving like one joined object.
low.examPointer: Name the direction of the distortion: the cation pulls the anion's electrons toward itself, never the reverse.

medium.restatement: Polarisation is the failure mode of the ionic ideal: the cation's field deforms the anion's electron density toward the internuclear axis, granting the bond partial covalent character and shifting the measured lattice energy off the purely electrostatic prediction.
medium.analogy: A strong magnet under one side of a water bed: the surface (electron cloud) bulges toward it, and the two objects no longer behave as independent units.
medium.examPointer: The theoretical-versus-measured lattice energy gap is the exam symptom; polarisation and its covalent character is the cause to quote.

modules.title: Polarising power versus polarisability
modules.opening: One property per side decides the outcome. Cations polarise in proportion to their charge density - charge divided by surface area - so small, highly charged cations wield the greatest polarising power: Li+ outguns K+, and Mg2+ outguns Na+. Anions suffer polarisation in proportion to their radius: the bigger the ionic radius, the more easily the cloud distorts, so Br- yields where Cl- resists.
keyPoints: A cation's polarising power rises with its charge density.
Charge density can be taken as the cation's charge divided by its surface area.
K+ polarises less than Li+ because its ionic radius is greater; Na+ polarises less than Mg2+ because its charge is smaller.
Small, highly charged cations have the greatest polarising power.
Anion polarisability rises with ionic radius - Br- is more polarisable than Cl-.

low.restatement: The attacker is the cation: small and multi-charged attackers squash best. The victim is the anion: big, floppy electron clouds squash easiest.
low.analogy: A stiletto heel (small, concentrated) dents a gym mat (large, soft) far more than a flat shoe dents a leather cushion.
low.examPointer: Keep the two vocabularies apart - polarising power belongs to cations, polarisability to anions.

medium.restatement: Charge density is the cation's field strength at the anion's surface: halving the radius or doubling the charge concentrates the pull, so Li+ (compact) and Mg2+ (doubly charged) dominate; anion distortion instead tracks how loosely its outer electrons are held, which scales with radius.
medium.analogy: Grip strength versus slipperiness: the cation's grip (charge density) meets the anion's slipperiness (cloud spread), and distortion is their product.
medium.examPointer: Compare pair-style: Li+ vs K+ is a radius argument, Na+ vs Mg2+ is a charge argument - quote the right variable per pair.

glossary.definition: The cation-induced distortion of an anion's electron density, adding covalent character to the ionic bond.
A cation's capacity to distort an anion, rising with its charge density.
An anion's susceptibility to distortion, rising with its ionic radius.
The cation's charge divided by its surface area.
